summary:
This run covered 18 evals, of which 2 were explicitly marked skipped (should_trigger: false, so no data to assess) and several more could only be measured on one variant because the other variant's run data was absent (e.g. guardduty-anomalous-invocation, scp-impact-before-applying, blocked-sometimes-no-account were without_skill-only; no-guardrail-on-production-path and draft-not-pinned-trap were effectively with_skill-only for assertions). These one-sided evals are absent data, not evidence that the missing variant performed poorly — they simply couldn't be compared.

Across the evals where both variants have data, a consistent pattern emerges: with_skill passed its "expected output" check and scored higher on per-assertion pass rates in most of the comparable evals (e.g. inactive-admin-key: with_skill 7/7 vs without_skill 2/7; pii-entry/pii-block-entry-with-only-action: with_skill 8/8 and 6/6 vs without_skill 4/8 and 3/6; version-limit-counts-draft: with_skill 7/7 vs without_skill 4/7; invocation-log-input-assessment-is-not-detection: with_skill 18/18 vs without_skill 14/18; grounding-score-near-threshold-invented-fact: with_skill 7/7 vs without_skill 5/7). In the two head-to-head evals with full LLM quality comparisons (tool-results-not-evaluated, grounding-score-near-threshold-invented-fact), with_skill was favored on accuracy/actionability/completeness; in one other (grounding-score-far-below-threshold) with_skill was favored on one criterion with the other two comparable; in guardrail-latency-streaming the quality comparison favored without_skill on all three criteria despite both variants tying on assertion pass rate (4/5 each) and expected-output pass. So the quality-comparison signal is mixed rather than uniformly one-sided, though it leans toward with_skill in most pairs where it was measured, with confidence generally medium-to-high.

On the earliest-listed evals (full-report-connected-accounts, api-key-inventory), neither variant met the expected output (0/1 for both), and several assertions always failed for both variants (e.g. naming each credential with grant/risk tier, citing docs.aws.amazon.com links, stating SCP/RCP scope limits) — these indicate assertion- or behavior-level gaps affecting both variants rather than a between-variant difference. Within these same evals, with_skill still passed more individual assertions than without_skill (e.g. 4/8 vs 2/8, and 4/11 vs 2/11), often on points like clearly stating the audit is read-only and not ending with a follow-up question/offer, where without_skill failed and with_skill passed.

Runtime and cost consistently differ: with_skill typically runs longer and costs more than without_skill across nearly every eval (e.g. full-report-connected-accounts 1m59s/$0.99 vs 1m13s/$0.61; api-key-inventory 1m55s/$0.96 vs 1m33s/$0.78; inactive-admin-key 1m29s/$0.74 vs 23s/$0.20; invocation-log-input-assessment-is-not-detection 27s/$0.23 vs 10s/$0.09). This is a consistent pattern worth noting as a tradeoff: where with_skill also shows higher assertion pass rates or favored quality judgments, the extra time/cost coincides with more complete or accurate responses; in the few cases where assertion rates tied or quality favored without_skill (guardrail-latency-streaming), with_skill's extra runtime did not come with a clear quality edge.

Several individual assertions are uniformly informative about the underlying task rather than about either variant: things like "no 12-digit number is present" or "no full access key ID is exposed" passed for both variants nearly everywhere (always_passes pattern), indicating these are not differentiating checks. Conversely, assertions like "cites AWS documentation with a docs.aws.amazon.com link" and "names each credential with grant and risk tier" failed for both variants repeatedly (always_fails pattern) in the account/credential-audit evals, suggesting a shared gap in that behavior regardless of variant.

Output-consistency (run-to-run stability) data is null/absent for all evals in this report, so no conclusion can be drawn about variance across repeated runs for either variant. Total failed iterations were 4 out of 34 runs, and the understanding_agent_space_skill feature was disabled for this run (not_waited: 34), so it contributes no information here.

Overall, in directly comparable evals, with_skill more often met the expected output and achieved higher assertion pass rates, and quality-judgment comparisons lean toward with_skill in most pairs, but not all (without_skill was favored on quality in guardrail-latency-streaming despite tied assertion scores). This comes with a consistent cost/runtime tradeoff in favor of without_skill (faster, cheaper) in every eval where metrics exist for both. A meaningful fraction of evals could only be assessed for one variant, limiting how broadly these patterns can be generalized, and several assertions and two whole evals reveal shared weaknesses or non-differentiating checks rather than a between-variant gap.
</summary>

full-report-connected-accounts.summary:
Both variants were tested on a single chat task (one run each), so all findings here rest on a very small sample and should be read as directional rather than statistically solid.

Trigger and expected output: The behavior under test fired successfully (1/1). Neither variant met the overall "expected output" bar (0/1 for both), and this was measured with high confidence, meaning the failure determination itself is reliable, not a weak judgment call.

Assertions (8 total per variant): with_skill passed 4/8 (50%), without_skill passed 2/8 (25%). Breaking this down:
- Two checks passed for both variants and tell us nothing about the difference: no 12-digit number appears, and no exposed/full access key ID is shown.
- Three checks failed for both variants, indicating shared gaps rather than one variant being deficient: naming each long-lived credential with its grant and risk tier, specifying which credential to fix first with concrete remediation steps, and stating that SCPs/RCPs and sts:AssumeRole are not evaluated. These look like areas needing work regardless of variant.
- Two checks diverged, both favoring with_skill: stating the audit is read-only without claiming to have changed/deleted/deactivated anything, and not ending with an offer or follow-up question (the latter judged with only medium confidence, so weigh that one more lightly).
- One check (citing AWS docs with a docs.aws.amazon.com link) failed for both.

Quality comparison: No side-by-side quality pairs could be evaluated (0 evaluated, 1 skipped), so there's no direct quality verdict available beyond the assertion-level data above.

Runtime and cost: with_skill took about 1m59s and cost ~$0.99; without_skill took about 1m13s and cost ~$0.61 — without_skill was meaningfully faster and cheaper in this single run. Context window utilization was low for both (6.9% vs 4.7%), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency: Not available for either variant (no repeated-run data), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed here.

Overall, this is a single-instance comparison with no quality-pair data and no consistency data. On the measured assertions, with_skill passed more checks than without_skill, including the two cases where they diverged, while without_skill was notably faster and cheaper. Several assertions failed for both variants, flagging likely shared gaps in the underlying behavior (credential naming/risk detail, remediation steps, scope-of-audit caveats, documentation citation) rather than a difference between the two.

api-key-inventory.summary:
This single chat-task eval was triggered successfully (1/1), but both variants failed to meet the expected output (0/1 for each), and this result was reported with high confidence, so it's a reasonably solid finding rather than a weak/low-confidence signal.

On the 11 individual assertions, with_skill passed 4/11 (36%) and without_skill passed 2/11 (18%) — with_skill passed more assertions overall, but neither variant did well in absolute terms.

Breaking down the assertion-level pattern:
- 6 of 11 assertions failed for both variants ("always_fails"), including core requirements like listing every long-term Bedrock API key found account-wide, describing each key's grant/risk tier and removal guidance, correctly stating that IAM doesn't report last-used time for API keys (in two separate phrasings), correctly handling expired-vs-inactive key re-enablement, and citing AWS documentation links, and not ending with a follow-up question. These shared failures point to gaps in the underlying behavior or possibly the assertions' phrasing, rather than a difference between the variants.
- 2 of 11 assertions passed for both variants ("always_passes"): never printing a full API key ID/ServiceCredentialAlias/ServiceUserName, and not exposing any full access key ID with recognizable prefixes. These are not differentiating since both variants handle them correctly.
- 2 of 11 assertions were split, with with_skill passing and without_skill failing: stating the audit was read-only with no changes made, and not containing any 12-digit number (likely an account ID leak check). Both of these were evaluated with high confidence, indicating without_skill in these specific runs made unsupported claims of action or exposed a 12-digit number (e.g., an account ID), while with_skill did not.

On runtime and cost, without_skill was faster (1m33s vs 1m55s) and cheaper ($0.78 vs $0.96), with lower context window utilization (4.8% vs 7.0%); neither showed any context compaction. These differences are modest in absolute terms but consistently favor without_skill on efficiency.

Quality comparison and output consistency data are not available: the quality comparison had 0 pairs evaluated (1 pair skipped), and output consistency is null for both variants, so no conclusions can be drawn on run-to-run stability or relative output quality beyond the assertion pass/fail data.

Overall, this is a single-task eval with limited statistical power. Both variants failed the overall expected-output check and share several core assertion failures, suggesting common gaps in the task behavior (e.g., documentation citations, key inventory completeness, last-used-time messaging). Where the variants diverge, with_skill passed on two assertions related to not overclaiming actions taken and not exposing a 12-digit number, while without_skill was modestly faster and cheaper. There is no quality-comparison or consistency data to weigh against these differences.

inactive-admin-key.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task involving an IAM access key security assessment. The triggering behavior under test fired successfully (1/1).

On the key outcome measure, with_skill met the expected output (1/1, 100%, high confidence) while without_skill did not (0/1, 0%, high confidence). Since both confidence ratings are "high," this difference appears to be a reliable finding rather than an artifact of weak measurement, though it is based on just a single task instance.

At the assertion level (7 assertions per variant, same underlying task), with_skill passed all 7 (100%), while without_skill passed only 2 of 7 (29%). Breaking this down:
- Two assertions passed for both variants ("always_passes" pattern): stating recommended remediation steps without claiming to have deleted/deactivated the key, and not exposing full access key IDs. These two assertions do not differentiate the variants.
- The remaining five assertions all follow a "with_skill passes, without_skill fails" pattern: explaining that inactive keys can be re-enabled and still pose risk, correctly reporting the key's actual status and risk rating, not ending with an offer/follow-up question, citing AWS documentation links, and avoiding exposure of a 12-digit number (likely an account ID). No assertions failed for both variants, and none passed only for without_skill.

On efficiency metrics, without_skill was notably faster (23s vs 1m29s) and cheaper ($0.20 vs $0.74), and used less of the context window (5.0% vs 13.6%). However, since without_skill failed to meet the expected output and most assertions, its speed and cost advantage comes alongside a substantial quality/correctness gap on this task, rather than being a pure efficiency win — this is a case where the lower-cost variant appears to have under-delivered on content.

No quality comparison data is available (0 pairs evaluated, 1 pair skipped), so no direct side-by-side quality judgment can be reported. Output consistency data is also absent (null) for both variants, so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed.

Overall, this is based on a single task/data point, which limits how much can be generalized. Within that limitation, with_skill satisfied the expected output and nearly all assertions, while without_skill satisfied only the two assertions that both variants passed and ran faster/cheaper. The efficiency metrics and the correctness/assertion results point in opposite directions for the two variants, and the lack of quality-comparison and consistency data means some dimensions remain unassessed.

tool-results-not-evaluated.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task about why a Bedrock guardrail shows zero interventions despite tool output passing through the conversation.

Trigger & expected output: The behavior under test fired as expected (1/1), and both with_skill and without_skill fully met the expected output (1/1, 100%), with high-confidence judgments and no low-confidence flags — this is a strong, reliable result for both.

Assertions: Both variants passed all 6 assertions (100% each), all with high confidence (or deterministic regex checks). Every individual assertion passed for both variants identically — none discriminate between them. This means on the specific correctness checks (explaining that tool results bypass the Converse API guardrail, not recommending filter-strength changes, placing the fix in the application layer, not falsely claiming to have called ApplyGuardrail, naming the toolResult field, and not exposing a raw account ID), the two variants are indistinguishable.

Quality comparison: Based on a single evaluated pair (no pairs skipped), with_skill was favored on all three criteria — accuracy, actionability, and completeness — with high average confidence. Since this rests on only one pair, it's a consistent signal but a narrow sample, so it should be weighed as suggestive rather than conclusive.

Runtime and cost: without_skill was notably faster (~10s vs ~20s) and cheaper (~$0.09 vs ~$0.17), and used somewhat less context window (5.2% vs 7.1%); neither variant exceeded the 30s runtime threshold. This is a clear efficiency advantage for without_skill.

Consistency: Output consistency data was not available (null) for either variant, so repeat-run stability cannot be assessed from this data.

Overall state: This looks like a tradeoff rather than a clear-cut outcome. Both variants are equally correct on all measured pass/fail assertions and both fully satisfy the expected output, so there's no difference in whether they get the core answer right. The one differentiator is a single quality-comparison pair where with_skill was favored on accuracy, actionability, and completeness, while without_skill ran about twice as fast and at roughly half the cost. Given the quality edge rests on just one evaluated pair, and consistency data is missing entirely, this should be read as a modest, low-sample-size quality signal favoring with_skill set against a clear efficiency advantage for without_skill, rather than a definitive difference in overall capability.

Per-assertion results (18 total checks) reinforce this: with_skill passed all 18 (100%), without_skill passed 14/18 (78%). These four failures for without_skill are substantive — they touch on accuracy of claims, correct severity rating, and citation completeness, which likely explains why without_skill also failed the overall expected-output check.

Overall: this is a single-task comparison, which limits how much can be generalized. Within that task, with_skill satisfied every assertion and the expected-output check, while without_skill failed four specific assertions tied to accuracy and completeness (unit-counting claims, verification-step framing, severity rating, and citation) and ran faster and cheaper.
